newsitem.title: CHINA: China urges more mergers, fewer bankruptcies.
newsitem.headline: China urges more mergers, fewer bankruptcies.

text.p: China's economic tsar Zhu Rongji has called for further mergers of lumbering state enterprises and fewer bankruptcies, major newspapers said on Thursday.
Zhu, a vice-premier who oversees the economy, also called for "strict controls on new industrial projects" to curb blind investment, the Financial News and the People's Daily said.
"(Blind investment)...is the most important reason for the difficulties of state enterprises," Zhu was quoted as saying during a visit to the booming southeastern province of Fujian last week.

The central government has pledged to restructure the economy next year to curb blind investment -- a rush by provinces to invest in high-profile industries resulting in overheated competition among state firms and mounting losses.
Economists say defiance from regional authorities would make the central government's attempt to restructure the economy difficult.
Zhu said the government favoured mergers of state enterprises over bankruptcies and frowned on foreign investment that would hurt state firms.
"We encourage more mergers and fewer bankruptcies because mergers...are conducive to preventing the loss of assets of state banks," Zhu was quoted as saying.
About one percent of China's 100,000 state enterprises are hopelessly in debt and unlikely to find buyers, according to some estimates.
The government has been reluctant to push many of these firms into bankruptcy due to fears of mass unemployment and social unrest.
On merging, acquiring companies must assume all the debts of acquired enterprises, but the former can stop paying interest on loans and can repay loans in instalments.
"This (debt repayment) policy can be a bit more favourable but debts cannot be written off," Zhu was quoted as saying.
The government has been struggling to limit the amount of bad debts that are written off.

An official of the cabinet's State Economic and Trade Commission said state commercial banks would write off 30 billion yuan ($3.6 billion) in bad debts of state enterprises in 1997, up from 20 billion yuan in 1996.
Vice-premier Zhu blamed the problems of state enterprises in part on imports and keen competition from foreign-funded firms as well as poor management.
"The guiding principle on foreign investment is to prevent attracting one (foreign-funded) company leading to a squeeze-out of a group of (state) enterprises," he said.
Zhu said instead of investing in industrial projects, funds should be channelled into basic infrastructure, including irrigation facilities.
Funds should also be spent on upgrading technology, improving product quality and strengthening research and development, he said.
Zhu called for a further crackdown on smuggling and tax evasion, which are also hurting state firms.
He said problems of state enterprises included higher production costs and lower profits.
But on the other hand, state enterprises now had their own funds and a freer hand to revamp themselves, Zhu said, adding that the difficulties of state firms should not be exaggerated.
